data.title: Acne excoriée — viva
data.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acne excoriée** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is acne excoriée?**
- Psychocutaneous disorder in which (usually mild) acne lesions — or even normal skin — are repetitively picked and squeezed, producing excoriations, crusted erosions, scars and post-inflammatory pigmentation out of proportion to the acne; also 'acné excoriée des jeunes filles' (young women)
- Part of skin-picking (excoriation) disorder in DSM-5 (obsessive-compulsive and related disorders)

**Q2. Associated psychological conditions.**
- Anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder, borderline personality traits, eating disorders, stress, perfectionism

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Crusted excoriations, erosions, linear scratch marks, atrophic and hypertrophic scars, PIH on face (forehead, cheeks, chin, along hairline), sometimes upper back; few primary acne lesions visible
- Patient often admits picking (unlike dermatitis artefacta)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Dermatitis artefacta (denies self-infliction), neurotic excoriations, acne vulgaris with secondary infection, impetigo, herpes simplex, prurigo, scabies, delusional infestation

**Q5. Management.**
- Empathetic approach; treat the underlying acne effectively (retinoid, BPO, isotretinoin if needed) to remove the 'trigger'
- Behavioural therapy: habit-reversal training, CBT, mindfulness; occlusive dressings/hydrocolloid patches, keeping nails short
- Psychiatric referral; SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline), N-acetylcysteine (glutamate modulator), low-dose antipsychotics in severe cases; treat PIH and scars once picking stops

**Q6. Which scale/tool helps assess skin picking?**
- Skin Picking Scale–Revised, Skin Picking Impact Scale; screen for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), OCD (Y-BOCS) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD questionnaire)

**Q7. What is the role of SSRIs and other drugs?**
- SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine — often higher doses) for underlying OCD/anxiety/depression; N-acetylcysteine 1200–3000 mg/day (glutamate modulator) helps picking behaviour; doxepin/hydroxyzine for itch; low-dose antipsychotics (olanzapine, aripiprazole) in resistant cases

**Q8. What is habit reversal therapy?**
- Behavioural therapy: awareness training (recognising triggers and urges), competing response (e.g. clenching fists, holding an object for 1 min), social support — combined with CBT; often the most effective long-term approach

**Q9. How do you manage the skin itself?**
- Treat even mild acne effectively (topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, oral antibiotics or isotretinoin when indicated — reduces triggers), occlusive hydrocolloid dressings to stop picking, keep nails short, treat secondary infection; later scar and pigment treatment (peels, lasers, microneedling) once picking stops

**Q10. Epidemiology.**
- Mostly young women (late adolescence to 30s); often mild acne with disproportionate excoriations; also in men with obsessive traits; comorbid anxiety, depression, OCD, BDD, eating disorders

**Q11. What is body dysmorphic disorder and its link?**
- Preoccupation with imagined or slight defects in appearance causing distress and repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, skin picking, camouflaging); 'acne dysmorphophobia'; poor satisfaction with cosmetic procedures; treat with SSRIs and CBT

**Q12. Describe the clinical appearance of lesions.**
- Excoriations, crusts, erosions, linear and angulated scars, post-inflammatory hyper/ hypopigmentation, few primary comedones/ papules; within reach — forehead, cheeks, chin; may be denied or admitted

**Q13. How do you communicate with the patient?**
- Non-judgemental, acknowledge distress, explain the cycle of picking and scarring, agree on goals; involve psychiatry/ psychology for CBT/ habit reversal; maintain regular follow-up

**Q14. What is 'picker's nodule'?**
- Chronic nodules from repeated picking (prurigo-like) — treat with intralesional steroid, occlusive dressings, cryotherapy, psychological intervention

**Q15. Prognosis.**
- Chronic and relapsing if underlying psychological issue untreated; with combined dermatology–psychiatry care many improve; scars may need later procedures

## Quick spotter facts
- Excoriations and scars out of proportion to few acne lesions in a young woman — acne excoriée
- Habit-reversal + treat acne + SSRIs/N-acetylcysteine

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Acne; psychocutaneous disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
